Chapter 3: War Arrives and Changes Everything.
When the first whispers of war reached England, it almost didn’t feel real. For most people, the conflict seemed far away—like something that would blow over soon, just a brief hiccup in everyday life.
But that illusion didn’t last. As the months dragged on, and casualty lists grew longer, war became impossible to ignore. The comfort and safety that once defined home were slowly replaced by a constant thread of fear and uncertainty.
If you were at university back then, everything changed in an instant. Young men who used to argue late into the night about philosophy or literature now lined up to enlist. The campus emptied out almost overnight—classmates, friends, all leaving for the front lines. And for the women who stayed behind, it was a strange mix of pride and helplessness. You watched the people you cared about march off, not knowing if you’d ever see them again.
Deciding to leave Oxford and join the war effort wasn’t easy. Imagine working so hard to earn your place at university, only to consider giving it up. But when the world around you is falling apart, the urge to do something—to help, to make a difference—can outweigh everything else. That’s why she volunteered as a nurse, determined to help however she could.
The hospital was nothing like the calm, orderly world of the university. The work was backbreaking, exhausting, and it took a toll emotionally too. Every day brought new wounded soldiers—sometimes in waves. The struggle to ease their pain, to bring a little comfort, was constant. And always, there was that gnawing fear: what if someone she knew ended up among the injured, or worse?
Still, the nurses found strength in each other. They swapped stories, offered shoulders to lean on, and even managed to laugh in the middle of all that chaos. But the horrors of war left deep scars. Imagine seeing young men, many barely older than yourself, broken and changed by battle. Receiving letters from the front, filled with longing and fear, made the war hit home in a way no newspaper ever could.
As time went on, the losses piled up. Friends and loved ones were killed or wounded, and grief became a part of daily life. Any sense of safety or certainty from before the war was gone. In its place grew a new awareness—how fragile life really is, and how deep human suffering can run.
And yet, even in the darkest times, there was a sense of purpose. Caring for the wounded, offering a little hope in all the despair—it was a way to fight back against the madness. You realize it’s not just about surviving; it’s about holding on to your humanity, even when the world seems bent on taking it away.
War changed everything. Old dreams and ambitions faded into the background. What truly mattered now were the bonds between people who endured together, the shared drive to make sense of a world turned upside down—and the hope that, out of all this wreckage, something better could be built.
